q: Your plotted position lies three-quarters of the way up from the lower parallel to the upper one. What is your latitude?
why: The parallels are 10' apart; three-quarters up is 7.5' north of 37°40'.

fig.note: Parallels of latitude on the chart

q: You span the dividers between the harbour and tonight's anchorage, then move them to the side of the chart. How far is it?
a: 18 nautical miles
why: On the latitude scale one minute = one nautical mile: 43' − 25' = 18'.

q: Your crew reads a position off a phone app. What latitude do you plot on the paper chart?
why: 0.75 of a degree × 60 = 45 minutes.

q: The log shows a steady 6 knots. How far through the water do you go in one hour?
a: 6 nautical miles
why: A knot is one nautical mile (1,852 m) per hour.

q: You sail due north as shown, with no tide or leeway. What latitude do you reach?
A navigation warning reports a drifting container. Is its position on the chart you have open?
a: No — just west of the chart's left edge
o: Yes — in the upper half of the chart
No — just north of the top edge
No — just east of the right edge
why: 019°55'E is 5' west of 020°00'E, the chart's western limit.

q: You anchor at high water. How much water will be under the keel at low water tonight?
why: At LW the depth falls by the range: 4.0 − 1.6 = 2.4 m, then minus the 1.8 m draft.

q: The rock off the point carries this drying height. What do you see as you pass at the time shown?
a: The rock showing 0.9 m above water
o: 0.9 m of water over the rock
2.1 m of water over the rock
why: Drying height 1.5 m above datum − 0.6 m of tide = 0.9 m still uncovered.

q: Your track crosses this drying patch. How much water is over it at the time shown?
why: Depth over a drying patch = height of tide − drying height: 1.6 − 0.4.

q: You approach a fixed bridge in the northern Adriatic. What is the clearance under it right now?
why: Clearance = charted clearance + (HAT − height of tide) = 12.0 + 0.7.

fig.title: Fixed bridge
lines: HAT is 1.1 m above chart datum

q: Feeling your way into a shallow bay, how much water is really under your keel?
why: Depth = 2.3 + 0.5 = 2.8 m below the surface; minus the 1.9 m draft.

q: On your metric chart a depth is printed as a large 2 with a small 5 set low beside it. What depth is that?
why: Metric charts show decimetres as a small figure: 2 with a small 5 = 2.5 m below chart datum.

q: Planning where to anchor, you find this printed in the bay. What is the seabed?
a: Sand and shells
why: Seabed abbreviations: S = sand, Sh = shells.

q: Off the headland the chart shows a small rock with this figure beside it. What is it?
a: A rock that never covers, 4 m high
o: A rock 4 m below the surface
A rock that dries 4 m at low water
A wreck with 4 m of water over it
why: A height in brackets beside a rock marks an islet that never covers.

q: The chart prints 'Foul' in the corner of the bay where you planned to drop anchor. What do you do?
a: Anchor elsewhere — debris may trap the anchor
o: Anchor there with extra scope for weed
Avoid it at low water only — it dries
why: Foul ground is no danger to passing boats but is to be avoided for anchoring.

q: The best-sheltered spot in the bay lies on this charted line. Where do you anchor?
a: Well clear of the cable
o: On it, with a tripping line
On it, if you leave at dawn
why: Never anchor over a charted cable: the anchor can snag or damage it.

q: Well offshore you pass the buoy labelled on the chart like this. What is it?
a: A data buoy recording weather and sea
why: ODAS = Ocean Data Acquisition System: a yellow data buoy; keep clear of it.

fig.note: Depths in metres · 20 M off the coast

q: Your planned route crosses this charted area. What do you do before you go?
a: Check navigational warnings for firing times
o: Cross only at night when it is quiet
Call the charter base for permission
why: Firing areas are live only at notified times: check NAVTEX and coast radio warnings.

q: Entering an unfamiliar harbour with rocks off the entrance, which of these charts do you use?
a: Chart 3 — the largest scale, most detail
o: Chart 1 — the bigger number, more detail
Chart 2 — a balance of area and detail
Any — they all show the same dangers
why: Use the largest-scale chart for pilotage: 1:12 500 shows the most.

q: Your charter boat's chart and this season's pilot book disagree about the harbour. Which do you trust?
a: The newer pilot book — and check by eye
o: The chart — it is the official document
The chart — pilot books are not surveyed
why: Harbours change: use the most recent information and confirm it visually.

fig.title: Harbour of Vathi
lines: with a light on its head

q: You want to know how up to date the paper chart aboard is. Where do you look?
a: The edition date and corrections in the margin
o: The year printed on the compass rose
The scale line in the title block
The latitude scale on the side
why: Edition date and Notices to Mariners corrections are printed in the bottom margin.

q: Your chart of a remote Dodecanese bay gives this source information. How do you treat its depths?
a: With caution — unsurveyed rocks may exist
o: As exact — old charts are re-checked
As too shallow — old surveys under-read
why: Old lead-line surveys can miss isolated rocks between soundings.

fig.title: Source diagram
lines: Surveyed in the 1880s by lead line

q: You take the variation from the chart's compass rose. What variation do you use?
Your chart's compass rose reads as shown. What variation do you use?
Close to your track the chart shows a small cross inside a dotted circle, with no depth given. What is it?
a: A rock of unknown depth, dangerous to you
o: A rock awash at chart datum
A wreck with over 20 m on it
why: A dotted danger line round a symbol marks a danger to surface navigation: keep clear.

q: An isolated rock near your route is marked 'PA' on the chart. How do you treat it?
a: Its position is approximate — give it room
o: Its depth is approximate — pass close
It has been removed — ignore it
It is a private area — keep out
why: PA = position approximate: the danger may lie some way from where it is drawn.

q: Near the strait the chart shows a stream arrow with feathers on one side of its shaft and '2kn' beside it. What does it tell you?
a: Flood stream, about 2 knots that way
o: Ebb stream, about 2 knots that way
why: Feathered arrow = flood stream, plain arrow = ebb; the figure is the spring rate.

q: Your plotted course is shown. What compass course do you give the helmsman?
why: True to compass: subtract east, add west: 120 − 3 + 2 = 119.

q: You take a bearing of the lighthouse for a fix. What true bearing do you plot?
why: The deviation card is for the steering compass only: 310 + 4°E variation = 314.

fig.title: Fix at 10:40
lines: You stand aft, clear of the engine

q: You are steering 090° by the steering compass. What is your true heading?
why: Compass to true: add easterly errors: 090 + 2°E deviation + 5°E variation.

q: In flat calm with no tide, the steering compass and the GPS disagree as shown. What is the likely cause?
a: Deviation from the metal and magnets stowed
o: Variation has changed since this morning
The GPS has lost its satellite fix
why: Iron and magnets near the compass add deviation: keep them well away.

fig.title: Motoring in flat calm
lines: in the locker under the compass

q: You arrive in a new sailing area and need the local magnetic variation. Where do you find it?
a: On the compass rose of the chart
why: Variation depends on place and year; the compass rose gives both.

q: You motor straight down this transit to check the steering compass. What is the deviation on this heading?
why: 315°T − 3°E = 312°M; the compass reads 317°, 5° more, so deviation is 5°W.

q: You take this bearing of the lighthouse. Which line do you draw from the light on the chart?
a: A line from the light on 230°T
o: A line from the light on 050°T
A line from the light on 140°T
A line from the light on 320°T
why: You lie on the reciprocal as seen from the light: 050 + 180 = 230.

q: You can identify these four objects. Which three give the best fix?
a: A, C and D
why: Choose objects near you and about 60°–120° apart; A and B lie on one line.

fig.note: B is a summit far inland, directly behind A

q: You are motoring east along the coast to take a three-point fix. In what order do you take the bearings?
a: P and R first, Q on the beam last
o: Q on the beam first, then P and R
Nearest first: Q, then P, then R
why: Beam bearings change fastest, so take them last; ahead and astern change slowly.

q: Your three bearings off Kythnos plot like this, a triangle almost a mile across. What do you do?
a: Re-take the bearings; assume the worst position
o: Plot the centre and carry on
Average it with the GPS position
Drop one bearing and use the other two
why: A large cocked hat means an error: wrong object, misread compass or deviation.

q: To pass safely south of the reef, what bearing of the church do you keep?
a: Less than 060°T
why: South of the line the church bears less than 060°; more means you are on the reef side.

q: Approaching on a leading line at night, you see the two lights like this. Which way do you alter?
a: To starboard, until they line up
o: To port, until they line up
Hold course; they line up closer in
Slow down until they line up
why: Move towards the front light: rear showing left of front means you are left of the line.

q: You have only one landmark in sight. How do you turn these bearings into a running fix?
a: Move the 10:00 line 5 M along 060°T
o: Cross the two bearings as they are
why: Transfer the first position line by the run between bearings, then cross it with the second.

q: You have this range and bearing of the headland. Where are you?
a: 2.5 M due west of the headland
o: 2.5 M due east of the headland
2.5 M due north of the headland
why: The headland bears 090° from you, so you lie 2.5 M along 270° from it.

q: Your pilotage plan uses this clearing bearing. What does the bearing you have just taken tell you?
a: You are on the dangerous side — alter away
o: You are safe — 5° is within error
You are exactly on the clearing line
Your compass needs a deviation check
why: NLT 190°: anything less than 190° puts you on the shoal side of the line.

fig.title: Clearing bearing
lines: (not less than) to clear the shoal

q: In haze you get one bearing of the light, and the echo sounder (corrected to chart datum) reads 20 m. What do you have?
a: A rough fix where the bearing meets the 20 m line
o: Only a position line — depth adds nothing
A full fix, as good as three bearings
why: A sounding gives a depth-contour position line; crossed with a bearing it gives a rough fix.

q: You take one bearing of a lighthouse and draw it on the chart. What do you have?
a: A position line — you are somewhere on it
why: One bearing gives one position line; you need a second line to cross it.

q: Your crew has marked the 14:00 position on the chart as a small circle round a dot. What kind of position is it?
a: A fix — an observed position
why: Chartwork symbols: circled dot = fix, triangle = EP, square = waypoint.

q: You plot your course and log distance from the last fix, then add the tidal stream and leeway. What do you have?
a: An estimated position (EP)
why: DR uses course and distance only; an EP adds tidal stream and leeway.

q: You leave the 10:00 fix as shown. Where is your 11:00 estimated position?
a: 6 M east and 1.5 M south of the fix
o: 6 M east and 1.5 M north of the fix
why: Plot the water track 6 M along 090°, then the tide 1.5 M towards 180°.

fig.note: Fix at the boat · no leeway

q: You leave at the time shown. When do you arrive?
You must reach the anchorage before dark. What average speed do you need?
a: 6.0 knots
why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 21 ÷ 3.5 h.

q: You are close-hauled as shown. What water track do you make?
why: Leeway pushes you downwind: wind on the port bow sets you to starboard, 040 + 5.

q: You want to make good the water track shown. What heading do you steer?
why: Leeway sets you north, downwind; steer 6° up into the wind to compensate.

q: Over an hour in open water, on several different headings, you see these readings. What is wrong?
a: The log under-reads — clean or calibrate it
o: A 1.2 kn current is helping you
The GPS over-reads in open water
Leeway is adding to your speed
why: A difference that stays the same on every heading is a log error, not a current.

q: Where is your DR position at 15:30?
a: 6.0 M west of the fix
why: 1.5 h × 4 kn = 6 M along the course; a DR ignores tide and leeway.

fig.note: Fix at the boat · no tide, no leeway

q: Which tidal stream do you take from this table?
a: 270°T at 0.9 knots
why: Read the HW−2 line at the neap rate; the direction is where the stream goes.

q: You want to cross the channel along the track shown. What course do you steer?
a: About 070°T
why: Aim up-tide about 20°: 2 kn ÷ 6 kn × 60 (1-in-60), so 090 − 20.

fig.note: Same stream for the whole crossing

q: Steering exactly the planned heading, you see the cross-track error grow as shown. What do you do?
a: Steer a few degrees to port to regain the track
o: Steer a few degrees to starboard of the track
Hold the heading; XTE corrects itself
Turn 90° to port until XTE is zero
why: A steady drift to starboard is a set; aim off to port to counter it.

fig.title: Chartplotter
lines: XTE 0.3 M, right of the track

q: The plotter and the compass show this. What is happening?
a: A stream or leeway is setting you east
o: A stream or leeway is setting you west
The GPS has lost its satellite fix
why: COG is your track over the ground; it lies to starboard of the heading, so you are set east.

q: Motoring north through a narrow strait, you read these speeds. What is the current doing?
a: About 1.7 kn against you
why: SOG = speed through water ± current: 5.5 − 3.8 = 1.7 kn on the nose.

q: How long will this passage take?
a: 3 h 00 min
why: Speed over ground = 5 − 1 = 4 kn; 12 ÷ 4 = 3 h.

fig.title: Passage up the channel
lines: Foul stream 1.0 kn all the way

q: You check the tidal stream atlas for your route. What do the figures beside the arrow mean?
a: 1.2 kn at neaps, 2.4 kn at springs
o: 1.2 kn at springs, 2.4 kn at neaps
1.2 kn at HW, 2.4 kn at LW
why: Atlas rates are in tenths of a knot, neap rate first, then spring rate.

q: Planning a cruise in Greece, where do you most need to work out the tidal stream before you go through?
a: The narrow Evripos strait at Chalkis
o: The open Aegean between Mykonos and Naxos
Any large bay, such as the Saronic Gulf
Nowhere — the Mediterranean has no tide
why: Med tides are small, but in narrow straits like the Evripos the stream runs at several knots.

q: Full moon was two days ago. What tides do you expect this week?
a: Springs — bigger range, stronger streams
why: Spring tides follow new and full moon by a day or two.

q: You must cross a shallow bar near low water. At which low water is there least water over it?
a: Low water at springs
o: Low water between springs and neaps
why: Springs have the biggest range: the highest highs and the lowest lows.

q: Using the rule of twelfths, what is the height of tide now?
why: Range 1.8 m; two hours after LW = 3/12 of it (0.45 m) + 0.4 m LW.

q: What is the earliest time you can cross the bar with the clearance you want?
why: Tide needed 2.0 + 0.5 − 0.6 = 1.9 m: a 1.5 m rise, half the range, 3 h after LW.

q: Heading into a marina in the Venetian lagoon, what do you expect of the water level compared with the tide tables?
a: Higher than predicted — a surge
o: Lower — the wind blows water out
Lower — low pressure lowers the sea
why: Low pressure and a long scirocco pile water into the northern Adriatic: acqua alta.

q: When is high water at your harbour?
why: Apply the time difference to the standard port: 10:40 − 35 min.

q: You plot GPS positions on this paper chart. What do you do?
a: Apply the shift in the note before plotting
why: GPS gives WGS84 positions; on an older-datum chart apply the stated shift.

q: Entering this Cycladic bay, the plotter shows your boat here. What do you do?
a: Navigate by eye, depth and bearings
o: Trust the plotter and turn back out
Steer until the screen shows water
why: Electronic charts of small Greek bays can be offset; the depth and the view are real.

q: Why do you write the position, log reading and course in the logbook every hour?
a: To plot a DR if the electronics fail
o: The charter company bills by distance
To calibrate the GPS each hour
The coastguard needs an hourly report
why: Hourly positions let you navigate on from the last known point if the GPS dies.

q: Planning the route on the plotter zoomed out, you see clear water all the way. What do you do before you rely on it?
a: Zoom in along every leg to check for dangers
o: Nothing — dangers show at every zoom
Move the route closer to the coast
why: Plotters hide small rocks and soundings at small zoom levels.

q: You set a GPS waypoint for a night arrival at a small harbour. Where do you put it?
a: In safe water off the entrance
o: On the end of the breakwater
On the charted position of the light
why: Waypoints go in clear water; pilot the last part in by eye and by the lights.

q: The plotter shows this bearing to the next waypoint. Ignoring deviation, what magnetic course do you steer?
why: True to magnetic: subtract easterly variation, 200 − 5.

q: Creeping through the marina at half a knot, you see the plotter's COG swing wildly from second to second. Why?
a: GPS course is unreliable at very low speed
o: The marina's steel pontoons cause deviation
The tidal stream keeps changing direction
why: COG comes from successive GPS positions; at walking pace small position errors swamp it.

q: You will enter an unfamiliar harbour at dusk. What do you prepare beforehand?
a: A plan of marks, bearings and turning points
o: Nothing — the plotter route is enough
A course straight at the entrance light
why: Write the plan before you arrive: what you will see, bearings to hold, where to turn.

q: What do you do about tonight's anchorage?
a: Choose another one sheltered from the south
o: Go anyway with extra chain out
Go anyway — pilot books are cautious
Anchor further in, close to the beach
why: A pilot-book warning matching the forecast: pick shelter from the forecast wind.

fig.title: Planning tonight's stop
lines: winds, swell rolls into the bay'

q: You plan a long passage along a rocky coast with few harbours. What must your passage plan include?
a: Ports of refuge along the way
o: Only the departure and arrival ports
A route as close inshore as possible
Only the waypoints for the autopilot
why: A plan needs bolt-holes in case of weather, breakdown or injury.

q: How do you round this breakwater head to enter the harbour?
a: Wide, then turn in
why: Breakwater heads often have rubble and shoals off them: round them wide.

fig.note: Harbour plan from the pilot book

q: How do you know when to make the turn in this plan?
a: When the light bears 090°M by hand-bearing compass
o: When the plotter shows half a mile to go
When the echo sounder falls below 10 m
When the chapel comes abeam to port
why: A planned bearing of an object on the beam is a precise, independent turning cue.

q: The pilot book says to approach the harbour from the south-west. Roughly what heading do you steer on the final approach?
a: About 045°
why: Coming from the south-west means heading north-east, 045°.

q: You lay your plotting instrument along the course line and line its grid up with a meridian. What kind of course do you read?
a: True
why: Meridians run to true north, so the course is true; then apply variation and deviation.

q: You read your course off the inner magnetic ring of the chart's compass rose, which is up to date. What must you still apply?
a: Deviation for that heading
o: Nothing — it is ready to steer
why: The inner ring already includes variation; only deviation remains.

q: Your GPS position and the echo sounder disagree like this. What do you do?
a: Slow down, head for deep water, take bearings
o: Trust the GPS — the sounder is wrong
Carry on — 8 m is plenty for you
why: When GPS and depth disagree, doubt the position and check it another way.

fig.title: Cross-check
lines: Chart depth at GPS position: 30 m

q: Your track passes over this charted wreck. What do you do?
a: Carry on, but don't anchor near it
o: Alter course — every wreck is a danger
Stop and sound the depth by hand
why: A wreck with 25 m over it is no danger to a yacht; just keep your anchor off it.

fig.note: Depths in metres below chart datum

q: How far off the light are you when it comes abeam?
why: Doubling the angle (45° to 90°): distance off = distance run = 0.5 h × 6 kn.

fig.title: Doubling the angle
lines: Speed over ground 6.0 kn, no stream

q: The chart prints 'Local magnetic anomaly' beside the island you are passing. What do you do?
a: Distrust the compass; cross-check by GPS and marks
o: Add an extra degree of variation
Nothing — it affects only big ships
why: A local anomaly can throw the compass several degrees off; navigate by other means.

q: Can you motor under this cable?
a: No — your air draft is 17.5 m
o: Yes — the mast is only 16.5 m
Yes — at low water you gain enough
Yes — mid-span the cable is higher
why: Air draft includes aerials, and the safe clearance must exceed it with room to spare.

q: Sailing to windward, how do you estimate your leeway?
a: Angle between the wake and the centreline
o: Log speed compared with GPS speed
why: Leeway is the angle between heading and water track, shown by the wake.

q: The marina's website says the next bay is 9 km away. How far is that in nautical miles?
a: About 4.9 M
why: One nautical mile = 1.852 km: 9 ÷ 1.852 ≈ 4.9.

q: How far off the intended track will you be at the end of the run?
a: About 1 M
why: 1-in-60 rule: 3° off over 60 M = 3 M off, so over 20 M = 1 M.
